Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National EU, CHRAJ call for stronger implementation of Ghana’s anti-corruption laws Source : myjoyonline 23 November 2026 10:20am ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The European Union (EU) and the Commission on Human Rights and Administrative Justice (CHRAJ) have called for stronger implementation and enforcement of Ghana’s anti-corruption laws and policies to improve transparency, accountability and public trust in state institutions.
They say although Ghana has made significant progress in establishing legal and institutional frameworks to combat corruption, weaknesses in implementation continue to undermine efforts to promote integrity in public service.
The call was made at a National Multi-Stakeholder Dialogue on Advancing Anti-Corruption Policy Uptake in Ghana, organised by the Ghana Anti-Corruption Coalition (GACC) in partnership with the Centre for Democratic Development (CDD-Ghana) and Transparency International Ghana, with support from the European Union.
Speaking at the event, Programme Officer of the EU, Davide Messina, said corruption and weak accountability systems pose serious threats not only to democratic governance but also to economic development, investment confidence and the delivery of essential public services.
He noted that gaps in transparency and accountability undermine competitiveness, discourage foreign investment and disproportionately affect vulnerable populations who depend on public services.
Mr Messina stressed that the EU remains committed to supporting Ghana's anti-corruption reforms, citing its financial and technical support for initiatives aimed at strengthening the rule of law, institutional accountability and the fight against corruption.
He disclosed that an EU-funded project, Strengthening Accountability, Rule of Law and Institutional Responsiveness in Ghana, had recently undertaken an assessment of gaps in existing public ethics and campaign financing regulations.
According to him, the findings provide an important basis for understanding weaknesses in the country's regulatory framework and identifying areas that require reforms.
He also highlighted the importance of collaboration between anti-corruption institutions and civil society organisations, insisting that citizens must be empowered to demand transparency and actively participate in exposing corruption.
"Educating citizens on the importance of transparency and accountability is equally important. Civil society organisations at national and local levels play a vital role in fostering a stronger sense of civic responsibility and encouraging active citizen participation," he said.
Meanwhile, CHRAJ has emphasised the need to move beyond the existence of anti-corruption laws and institutions to ensure their effective implementation and enforcement.
In a speech read on behalf of the Commissioner of CHRAJ, Joseph Whittal, by the Commission's Technical Advisor, Stephen Azantilow, the Commission said the effectiveness of Ghana's anti-corruption framework ultimately depends on how consistently existing laws are enforced and how responsive the institutions mandated to uphold them are.
He said Ghana had established several constitutional, legislative and institutional mechanisms to promote integrity in public life, but their existence alone does not guarantee accountability.
The Commissioner cited Article 218 of the 1992 Constitution, which mandates CHRAJ to investigate complaints of corruption and abuse of power by public officers, as well as suspected cases of corruption and misappropriation of public funds.
He further referenced Chapter 24 of the Constitution, particularly Article 284, which prohibits public officers from placing themselves in situations where their personal interests conflict, or are likely to conflict, with the performance of their official duties.
He said the provisions underline the importance of ethical conduct and integrity in public office, stressing that public officials must be held to the standards established by the Constitution.
